claims.text: Moderate cold rolling can simultaneously improve the strength and ductility of eutectic high-entropy alloys.
The initial alloy is eutectic AlCoCrFeNi2.1 produced by vacuum induction melting.
The as-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy has alternating fcc and B2 lamellae.
The as-cast alloy has an inter-lamellar spacing of about 2 μm.
An approximately 8% thickness reduction by cold rolling is a moderate deformation treatment applicable to this alloy.
The proposed effect should hold for room-temperature tensile testing at a strain rate around 1 × 10^-3 s^-1.
Cold rolling by about 8% decreases the inter-lamellar spacing.
Cold rolling by about 8% increases dislocation density at the fcc/B2 interfaces.
The fcc/B2 interphase boundaries impede dislocation glide and thereby increase strength.
The retained ductile fcc phase and distributed dislocations enhance strain hardening and help maintain ductility.
The as-cast alloy has a tensile strength or fracture stress of approximately 944 MPa.
Eight percent cold rolling is expected to increase ultimate tensile strength to approximately 1265 MPa.
After cold rolling, the alloy is expected to retain around 10% tensile elongation.
The as-cast alloy has an engineering elongation of 25.6%.
Excessive cold deformation could cause damage or embrittlement.
The proposed benefit may be limited to eutectic HEAs with a similar dual-phase lamellar architecture.
The quantitative ductility response may vary with processing conditions and alloy composition.
Failure to obtain both statistically significant strength increases and maintained or improved ductility would falsify the hypothesis.
Failure to observe lamellar refinement and increased interfacial dislocation density would falsify the proposed mediation mechanism.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis claims improved or maintained ductility, and the falsification rule requires maintained or improved ductility, but the predicted elongation is around 10% whereas the cited as-cast baseline is 25.6%. Thus the quantified prediction represents a substantial ductility decrease.

The conditions call for testing at about 1 × 10^-3 s^-1 under conditions identical to the as-cast control, while the cited record reports cold-rolled specimens tested at 2 × 10^-3 s^-1. The proposed experiment does not explicitly resolve this difference.
